hints: Apply $x=3$ at $\theta=\pi/4$, then exponentiate and simplify to express $x$ explicitly.
walkthrough:
Separate the variables in $(3 + \cos 2\theta)\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = x\sin 2\theta$ by dividing by $x(3 + \cos 2\theta)$ and multiplying by $\mathrm{d}\theta$:
$$\dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{3 + \cos 2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Observe that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(3 + \cos 2\theta) = -2\sin 2\theta$. Multiply and divide the right-hand integral by $-2$:
$$\int \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{3 + \cos 2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{-2\sin 2\theta}{3 + \cos 2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(3 + \cos 2\theta)$$

Combine into the integrated equation with constant of integration $c$:
$$\ln x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(3 + \cos 2\theta) + c$$

Substitute the initial condition $\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$ and $x = 3$ to find $c$:
$$\ln 3 = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(3 + \cos\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) + c = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(3 + \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) + c$$

Substitute $c = \dfrac{3}{2}\ln 3$ back into the solution:
$$\ln x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(3 + \cos 2\theta) + \dfrac{3}{2}\ln 3 = \ln\left((3 + \cos 2\theta)^{-1/2}\right) + \ln\left(3^{3/2}\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{3^{3/2}}{\sqrt{3 + \cos 2\theta}}\right)$$

Simplify $3^{3/2} = \sqrt{3^3} = \sqrt{27}$ and exponentiate both sides to express $x$ explicitly in terms of $\theta$:
$$x = \sqrt{\dfrac{27}{3 + \cos 2\theta}} \quad \left(\text{or } x = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3 + \cos 2\theta}}\right)$$

ai_rubric.Solving Separable Differential Equations: Derives term $\ln x$. Derives term $-\frac12\ln(3+\cos2\theta)$, or equivalent. The final result is $\displaystyle x=\sqrt{\frac{27}{3+\cos2\theta}}$.

hints: To minimise this positive expression, maximise the denominator $3+\cos2\theta$.
Use the greatest possible value of $\cos2\theta$ and simplify the resulting exact square root.
walkthrough:
Consider the expression for $x$ obtained in part (i):
$$x = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3 + \cos 2\theta}}$$
Since the numerator $3\sqrt{3}$ is a positive constant, $x$ takes its minimum value when the denominator $\sqrt{3 + \cos 2\theta}$ takes its maximum value.
The maximum value of the cosine function is $\cos 2\theta = 1$.
